title: Post-quantum standards are not migration
summary: A qualitative technology-readiness map built from Published NIST standards and preliminary PIV specification records, showing how post-quantum cryptography becomes migration work while institution-level implementation remains unresolved.
map_question: How do post-quantum cryptography standards become operational migration work, and where does FTFN still lack implementation evidence?
interpretation_boundary: This map connects final PQC standards, federal direction, implementation requirements, and a preliminary credential-specification artifact. It does not prove that an agency, contractor, vendor, critical-infrastructure operator, or local system has completed post-quantum migration.

nodes.label: Quantum
nodes.note: The topic frame connects quantum risk, standards, infrastructure obligations, and human-system migration choices.

nodes.label: NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Project
nodes.note: A Tier 1 standards source for PQC standards and migration context.

nodes.label: NIST PQC standards signal
nodes.note: A Published security signal framing PQC as near-term migration work rather than distant theory.

nodes.label: Executive Order 14412
nodes.note: A Tier 1 directive establishing federal leadership, system-transition, pilot, guidance, and procurement deadlines.

nodes.label: OMB M-26-15
nodes.note: A Tier 1 implementation memorandum requiring agency plans, risk prioritization, modernization, and vendor-readiness work.

nodes.label: PIV post-quantum working drafts
nodes.note: A Published preliminary specification artifact that proposes ML-DSA and ML-KEM support for federal identity credentials without claiming a final requirement or deployed capability.

nodes.label: HQC backup-algorithm selection
nodes.note: A Published selection-stage record that adds mathematical diversity upstream of a draft and final standard.

nodes.label: Post-Quantum Cryptography
nodes.note: A source-backed technology profile for standards, algorithms, validation, and migration practices.

nodes.label: Standards adoption
nodes.note: Standards must be adopted through inventories, procurement rules, software updates, validation, and vendor support.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity migration
nodes.note: Migration risk is shaped by legacy systems, stored encrypted data, critical infrastructure exposure, staffing, and execution timelines.

nodes.label: Institution-level migration evidence
nodes.note: FTFN now has federal requirements and deadlines but still needs agency inventories, plans, procurement records, vendor readiness, and completed milestones.

links.note: The Quantum topic explicitly includes post-quantum cryptography and migration risk.
The Published standards signal cites NIST PQC as its source.
The signal and technology profile share the same primary source and topic context.
The Published PIV record cites Executive Order 14412 as part of the federal policy context for credential migration.
The Published PIV record cites OMB M-26-15 as part of the federal planning, modernization, and vendor-readiness context.
The working drafts translate NIST-standardized algorithms into proposed credential data models, interfaces, and migration behavior.
The preliminary specification narrows one implementation layer but does not supply final requirements, validated products, completed pilots, issued credentials, or system-transition evidence.
HQC is a selected backup key-encapsulation algorithm based on different mathematics from ML-KEM.
Algorithm selection strengthens the standards-diversity trail but does not supply a final standard, product support, procurement, or migration evidence.
The technology record lists standards adoption as a dependency.
The current record base supports cybersecurity and migration framing, but not sector-specific execution claims.
Institution-level migration evidence remains an open evidence gap.

what_this_map_supports: FTFN can distinguish standards progress from operational migration progress.
FTFN can show how standards, executive direction, OMB implementation requirements, security signals, a technology profile, and an evidence gap fit together.
Federal direction, implementation requirements, and preliminary PIV specifications expose a dated migration and standards stack.
The HQC selection adds a bounded standards-diversity milestone without changing the current ML-KEM migration baseline.
The PIV working drafts make credential data models and interfaces inspectable while remaining upstream of formal standards and deployment.
Post-quantum cryptography can be tracked as infrastructure migration work without numeric scoring.
what_this_map_does_not_prove: It does not prove that any institution has completed post-quantum migration.

It does not prove agency plan acceptance, final PIV requirements, validated products, vendor readiness, procurement compliance, cryptographic inventory completeness, migrated systems, or critical-infrastructure execution.
It does not rank quantum risk or create a 42/59 score.
